subtitle: An IP address is a 32-bit number cut into “which network” and “which host”. Every subnetting question is where to cut.

addr.body:
An IP address is like the postal address on a letter you send: the first part names the town, the last part names the house. An IPv4 address is 32 bits written as four decimal bytes. The subnet mask (or prefix length /n) marks the first n bits as the network part; the rest identify the host.

Originally the split was fixed by class: A (first bit 0, /8), B (10, /16), C (110, /24), D (1110, multicast), E (reserved). Modern CIDR allows any prefix length. As the figure shows, 192.168.10.77/26 is on network 192.168.10.64 with broadcast 192.168.10.127 and 62 usable hosts. Which class is 172.16.5.9 in the original classful scheme? The first byte 172 starts with bits 10, so class B.
keynotes: An IPv4 address is 32 bits written as four decimal bytes; the subnet mask (or prefix length /n) marks the first n bits as the network part.
Classes: A (first bit 0, /8), B (10, /16), C (110, /24), D (1110, multicast), E (reserved); CIDR allows any prefix length.
192.168.10.77/26 is on network 192.168.10.64 with broadcast 192.168.10.127 and 62 usable hosts.

subnet.body:
Three numbers describe any subnet, and you can compute them in your head with practice. AND the address with the mask to get the network address. Set all host bits to 1 for the broadcast address. The usable hosts lie between them: 2h − 2 where h is the number of host bits (the all-zeros and all-ones addresses are reserved).

Do 192.168.10.77/26. The last byte 77 = 01001101, and /26 leaves 6 host bits. Network: zero the host bits → 01000000 = 64. Broadcast: set them → 01111111 = 127. So the range is 192.168.10.64 to 192.168.10.127, and usable hosts = 2⁶ − 2 = 62. How many usable hosts in a /27? Five host bits give 2⁵ − 2 = 30.
keynotes: AND the address with the mask to get the network address; set all host bits to 1 for the broadcast address.
Usable hosts are 2^h − 2 where h is the number of host bits.
For 192.168.10.77/26 the network is 64, the broadcast is 127 and there are 2⁶ − 2 = 62 usable hosts.

vlsm.body:
Giving every department the same size block wastes addresses, like booking the same size hall for a wedding and a tea party. VLSM gives each network just the block it needs. The recipe: sort requirements largest first, give each the smallest power-of-two block that fits its hosts + 2, and place blocks back to back so they stay aligned.

From 192.168.1.0/24 for 100, 50, 20 and 10 hosts you get 192.168.1.0/25 192.168.1.128/26 192.168.1.192/27 192.168.1.224/28. Why allocate the largest subnet first? Because large blocks need the strictest alignment, and placing them first leaves no awkward gaps.
keynotes: VLSM gives each network just the block it needs.
Sort requirements largest first, give each the smallest power-of-two block that fits its hosts + 2, and place blocks back to back so they stay aligned.

special.body:
There are not enough IPv4 addresses for every device you own, let alone the whole earth, so clever workarounds were invented. Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are not routed on the Internet. NAT rewrites a private source address and port to the router’s public address, keeping a table so replies return to the right host. That is why several hosts can share one public IP.

Know the three ways of sending: unicast goes to one host, broadcast to all hosts on a network, multicast (224/4) to a group. IPv6 (128-bit, written in hex) removes the address shortage and most need for NAT; transition uses dual stack, tunnelling or translation. In the figure, the NAT table maps the public port back to the private host.
keynotes: Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are not routed on the Internet; NAT rewrites a private source address and port to the router’s public address using a table.
Unicast goes to one host, broadcast to all hosts on a network and multicast (224/4) to a group.
IPv6 (128-bit, written in hex) removes the address shortage; transition uses dual stack, tunnelling or translation.

magic.body:
Here is a shortcut you will love in exams. For a mask whose interesting byte is m, the block size (the “magic number”) is 256 − m. Subnets start at multiples of it. For /26 the mask byte is 192, the block size 64, so subnets start at 0, 64, 128, 192, and 77 falls in the block starting at 64.

Try 10.1.1.130/27. /27 means mask byte 224, so the block is 32. Multiples of 32: …, 96, 128, 160. 130 lies in the block starting at 128, so the network is 10.1.1.128, the broadcast 10.1.1.159, and the usable hosts .129–.158. And the block size of a /28? The mask byte is 240, so 256 − 240 = 16.
keynotes: The block size (magic number) is 256 − m for a mask byte m, and subnets start at multiples of it.
For /26 the mask byte is 192, the block size 64, so subnets start at 0, 64, 128, 192.
10.1.1.130/27 has block 32, so network 10.1.1.128, broadcast 10.1.1.159 and usable hosts .129–.158.

summary.body:
Three lines, and you can solve any subnetting question.

  • Network = address AND mask; broadcast = host bits all 1; hosts = 2ʰ − 2.
  • VLSM: largest block first.
  • NAT trades address space for a translation table.
keynotes: Network = address AND mask, broadcast = host bits all 1, and hosts = 2ʰ − 2.
With VLSM, allocate the largest block first.
NAT trades address space for a translation table.
